units.title: Prompt tokenization and preprocessing as request work
outcomes: Explain where prompt tokenization and detokenization sit in a serving request and why their cost lands in TTFT and streaming gaps.
Measure tokenizer and detokenizer CPU time with a sampling flame graph and name the hottest functions.
State the prompt lengths and conditions under which tokenization can be ignored in a baseline.
units.why: Tokenization runs on the host before the first device kernel, and detokenization runs between streamed tokens. A slow tokenizer looks exactly like slow prefill or ragged decode in a naive trace.

next.note: Carry the tokenizer span into the TTFT decomposition.
Fix prompt lengths in tokens before comparing timings.

study.title: A CPU-bound tokenizer as the bottleneck
study.locator: Profiling, Debugging, and Tuning Inference Performance (pp. 959 to 964): the host-CPU-at-100-percent tokenization example and moving it to a GPU tokenizer or custom kernel
study.depth: Read only the host-CPU tokenization example. Leave cache-hit tuning and tiered-cache sizing for the KV sections.

study.title: Where tokenization enters TTFT
study.locator: Frontend Stats Collection: arrival_time starts when tokenization begins, and TTFT is measured relative to it

study.title: CPU flame graphs with py-spy
study.locator: README Usage: py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python myprogram.py for a flame graph, and py-spy top for the live view

focus: Tokenization and detokenization are host work inside the request path. Tokenization adds to TTFT and scales with prompt length; detokenization adds to gaps between streamed tokens and scales with output length.
vLLM starts the TTFT clock when tokenization begins, so tokenizer time is inside TTFT by definition, not beside it.
A flame graph attributes host time to functions. Look for tokenizer encode and decode calls with regex or Python-loop frames, not device kernels.
Ignoring tokenization is a stated assumption, not a default. It fails for long prompts, slow tokenizers and per-token detokenization in streaming.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the request path from arrival through tokenization, queue, prefill, first-token sampling and detokenization, and mark which spans vLLM counts in TTFT. Then profile a local tokenize and detokenize loop with py-spy record and name the two hottest frames.
traps: Reading TTFT as prefill time. TTFT includes queueing, tokenization, scheduling and host overhead around the prefill kernels.
Profiling the tokenizer once with a cold import. Import and cache warmup dominate the first call, so profile steady-state calls on your prompt distribution.
Detokenizing each token independently in analysis code. Streamed text uses incremental detokenization state, so naive per-token decoding can disagree with what the user saw.

selfTest.q: Where does vLLM start the TTFT clock?
selfTest.a: When tokenization begins on the frontend. Tokenizer time is inside TTFT by construction.

selfTest.q: A flame graph shows most request-wall time in a Python regex function under prefill-heavy load. Is the prefill kernel slow?
selfTest.a: There is no evidence for that. The host tokenizer or preprocessing is the bottleneck, and the device may be idle waiting for work.

selfTest.q: When is it safe to ignore tokenization in a baseline?
selfTest.a: Only when you measured it small against TTFT on your prompts, with the tokenizer, cache state and lengths recorded. Long prompts or per-token detokenization break the assumption.

selfTest.q: Why launch the process under py-spy record instead of attaching to a running server with a process id?
selfTest.a: Attaching to a process you did not start usually needs elevated permissions. Launching under py-spy record avoids that restriction.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: tokenizer and detokenizer spans in the request lifecycle trace, with a flame-graph attachment for the hottest host frame.
units.stopWhen: You can point to the tokenizer span inside a TTFT trace and to the hottest tokenizer frame in your own flame graph, and state the prompt lengths where ignoring it stops being safe.

fit.note: Coverage failed for CPU flame-graph tooling; py-spy supplies the verified record and top workflow beside the pool's tokenizer-bottleneck example.

units.title: Prefill parallelism, the decode dependency and decode shapes
outcomes: Explain why prefill exposes sequence parallelism while decode is sequential across generated tokens.
Derive the per-step shapes of a decode step as matrix-vector-like work against a growing KV cache.
Predict how prompt length and output length move prefill work versus decode steps.
units.why: Every phase-separated measurement in this section assumes this split. If you cannot say which work is parallel and which is forced sequential, no TTFT or TPOT number means anything.

next.note: Place the prefill and decode shapes on a roofline.
See how batching reuses decode weight loads.

study.title: Prefill parallelism and the decode dependency
study.locator: Section 2.2, Inference Setup (p. 3): prefill as one forward pass parallel over batch and prompt tokens, decode as sequential forward passes with one new token each

study.title: Why decode cannot parallelize across time
study.locator: Section 2.1 (p. 3): decode cannot batch across the sequence, and KV cache load per generated token grows with context and batch

study.title: Decode shapes: one row at a time
study.locator: Applying Arithmetic Intensity Analysis to the LLM Prefill and Decode Phases (pp. 183 to 185): Figure 5-16 with M = s for prefill and M = 1 for decode
study.depth: Use the shape argument and the regime verdicts only. Recompute the arithmetic-intensity numbers yourself: the printed formula drops parentheses and understates short-sequence values by about half.

focus: Treat the Two regimes: prefill and decode unit as read. This unit adds the per-step shapes and the serving measurement consequences.
Prefill processes all prompt tokens together, so its work grows with prompt length but parallelizes across the sequence. Decode produces one token per step because each token needs the previous one.
A decode step loads the full weight set plus the whole KV cache to produce one token and append one entry: matrix-vector-like shapes with almost no reuse.
The KV cache turns quadratic recomputation into linear per-step reads. Without it, each decode step would rescan the full prefix.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the dependency chain for generating four tokens from a prompt, stating what each step reads and appends. Then solve the TensorTonic uniform two-position public case by hand to get output [[[4]]].
traps: Calling decode compute-bound because the model is large. A decode step loads weights and cache for one token, so size raises the bytes moved, not the reuse.
Assuming prefill cost repeats per token. Prefill runs once; decode steps each read the cache but never redo the full prompt pass.
Treating batching as parallelism across time. Batching parallelizes across requests; the output steps of one request stay sequential.

selfTest.q: Why can prefill use large matrix multiplies while decode cannot?
selfTest.a: Prefill holds all prompt tokens at once, so the multiply has M = s rows. Decode holds one new token because each token depends on the previous one, so M = 1.

selfTest.q: What does one decode step read?
selfTest.a: The full weight set once plus the KV cache for all cached positions, to produce one token and append one entry.

selfTest.q: In the TensorTonic public case with query 0 and keys 1 and 2, why is the output 4?
selfTest.a: Both scores are 0, so the weights are 0.5 and 0.5. Then 0.5 x 2 + 0.5 x 6 = 4.

selfTest.q: A batch holds 8 requests that each generate 50 tokens. How many sequential steps does each request need?
selfTest.a: 50. Batching does not shorten any single request's dependency chain.

practice.note: Solve the public cases by hand first, then implement. The grouped-query head mapping is the bridge to the attention-variant units.

units.stopWhen: You derive the decode-step shapes without notes and your kv_cache_decode_step passes all public cases.

units.title: Compute, bandwidth, launch, capacity and queue-bound regimes
outcomes: Derive arithmetic intensity for a matmul and place prefill and decode work on a roofline for your GPU.
Explain the compute, bandwidth, launch, capacity and queue-bound regimes and how batching moves each boundary.
Predict the bottleneck for short and long prompts with small and large batches before profiling.
units.why: Regime classification is the prediction half of this section's checkpoint. Every later claim about a stall or a speedup is checked against the regime you declared first.

next.note: Move the boundaries with batch size and chunked prefill.
Turn regime predictions into residuals and goodput.

study.title: Roofline and arithmetic intensity, recomputed
study.locator: Boundaries of GPU Compute and Memory Bandwidth (pp. 178 to 180), Arithmetic Intensity in Matrix Multiplications (pp. 181 to 183) and Applying Arithmetic Intensity Analysis to the LLM Prefill and Decode Phases (pp. 183 to 185)
study.depth: Recompute Table 5-9 and Table 5-10 with the parenthesized formula M x N x K / (M x K + K x N + M x N). The printed formula omits the parentheses and its last denominator term is wrong: at h = 4096 the correct prefill values are about 62 and 410 for s = 64 and 512, and the correct decode value is about 1.0, not 0.5. The verdicts are unchanged.

study.title: Cost, MFU and the latency trade-off
study.locator: Section 2.1 (p. 3) and Section 4.4 with Tables 2 and 3 (pp. 9 to 10): small batches give low latency at worse MFU and higher cost, and the low-latency versus high-throughput configurations

study.title: Small batches and the launch floor
study.locator: Inference Troubleshooting Recipes with Table 16-1 (pp. 973 to 978): the below-50-percent-SM-utilization small-batch row, which prescribes larger batches and fused kernels before reaching for the profiler

study.title: The saturation knee
study.locator: Week 5: the concurrency sweep at 1, 2 and 4 up to 128, and the knee where throughput saturates while latency degrades

focus: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. The ridge is peak FLOPs per second divided by peak bytes per second, and work below it is bandwidth-bound.

Prefill intensity grows with sequence length while decode intensity stays near 1 FLOP per byte at any length. At very small shapes time stops falling with bytes: that flat floor is the launch-bound regime.
Batching raises intensity by reusing each weight load across requests, which moves the bandwidth boundary but never removes the sequential decode chain.

Capacity-bound means the KV cache does not fit, so the batch or the lengths must shrink. Queue-bound means waiting requests grow while the device stays busy. Diagnose both from occupancy and waiting counts, not from kernel timings.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(\text{AI} = M N K / (M K + K N + M N)\) for a matmul, evaluate it for \(M = s\) and \(M = 1\) at \(h = 4096\) and \(s = 64\), and place both points against a ridge of 419 FLOPS per byte.
traps: Quoting the book's Table 5-10 decode value of 0.5. The printed denominator is wrong and the correct value is about 1.0. Both sit far below any GPU ridge, so the verdict stands but the number does not.
Comparing intensities across precisions or tokenizers without restating units. Bytes per element and tokens per request change the numbers, so a ratio without its setup is not comparable.
Naming a regime from device utilization alone. Low SM use with full memory is capacity-bound; low SM use with empty memory and a growing queue is queue-bound.

selfTest.q: What are the units of arithmetic intensity and of the roofline ridge?
selfTest.a: FLOPs per byte for intensity. The ridge is peak FLOPs per second divided by peak bytes per second, also FLOPs per byte.

selfTest.q: At h = 4096 on a ridge of 419, which corrected Table 5-10 prefill values are compute-bound?
selfTest.a: Only s = 4096 at about 1365. The corrected 62 at s = 64 and 410 at s = 512 are still bandwidth-bound, as is decode at about 1.0.

selfTest.q: Why does batching move the bandwidth boundary?
selfTest.a: One weight load serves B tokens instead of one, so FLOPs per byte rise with B while the sequential steps per request stay fixed.

selfTest.q: How do you tell capacity-bound from queue-bound without a profiler?
selfTest.a: Capacity-bound shows full memory with small admitted batches. Queue-bound shows waiting requests growing while the device stays busy. Check occupancy and waiting counts.

practice.locator: Run the roofline plot and the attention arithmetic-intensity cells for your GPU; reproduce the N = 4096, d = 128 example at about 31 ops per byte and sweep batch size to the compute-bound crossover
practice.note: The notebook's attention accounting follows its book's model. Check it against your matmul derivation rather than treating it as a measured result.

units.stopWhen: Your hand-derived intensities match the corrected table values, and your roofline plot puts prefill and decode on opposite sides of the ridge for a long prompt.

units.title: Batch size, sequence shape, chunked prefill and phase interference
outcomes: Explain how batch size and sequence shape move work between bandwidth-bound and compute-bound execution.
Explain chunked prefill and how unchunked prefills stall ongoing decodes.
Predict the interference a long-prompt request inflicts on concurrent decode streams.
units.why: Batching is the main lever on serving cost, and naive batching taxes decode latency. Chunked prefill exists because one long prompt once stalled every other request on the server.

next.note: Attribute interference delays to queue, prefill or decode spans.
Design the mixing and chunking policy in the scheduler.

study.title: Chunked prefill and stall-free batching
study.locator: Sarathi-Serve: Design and Implementation: Chunked-prefills and Stall-free batching with Determining Token Budget; the prefill-prioritizing schedule that stalls ongoing decodes as the negative example
study.depth: Skip the pipeline-parallel sections and the Evaluation capacity numbers. Treat the reported capacity gains as the paper's result on its hardware, not as your target.

study.title: Batch size moves the bottleneck
study.locator: Section 4.1 with Figures 6 and 7 (p. 8): decode stays on the stationary layout while prefill switches layout by tokens per batch

study.title: Chunked prefill as the preemption fix
study.locator: Week 5 decision point: when TTFT spikes and waiting requests climb before the target concurrency, stop and tune maximum sequences, GPU memory utilization and chunked prefill first

focus: A batch mixes prefill tokens and decode tokens in one iteration. Prefill tokens bring large parallel work; decode tokens bring one step each with their full cache reads.
An unchunked long prefill occupies iterations that ongoing decodes also need, so their inter-token gaps spike. Chunked prefill splits the prompt into near-equal chunks that fit beside decodes.
The token budget caps prefill tokens per iteration. A smaller budget protects decodes but stretches the new request's TTFT: that trade-off is the whole design.
Splitting is not free. Chunked attention recomputes partial results across chunks, so read Overhead of chunked-prefills for what the split costs.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, sketch one iteration with a 4000-token prefill joining ten ongoing decodes, then the same arrival under a 512-token chunk budget, and state which requests slow down in each case and why.
traps: Assuming bigger batches always help both phases. Bigger batches raise throughput but an admitted long prefill still stalls the decodes it shares iterations with.
Treating the chunk budget as a latency knob for the new request only. The budget sets every concurrent decode's worst gap too.
Reading the paper's capacity multiples as expected gains. They hold for the paper's models, hardware and tail-latency constraints; your matrix decides yours.

selfTest.q: Why does one long prompt hurt ongoing decodes under prefill-prioritizing scheduling?
selfTest.a: Its full prefill occupies whole iterations, so decode steps wait. The waits appear as inter-token gaps on unrelated requests.

selfTest.q: What does chunked prefill change about that iteration?
selfTest.a: Only one chunk of the prompt joins each iteration, bounded by the token budget, so decodes keep making progress every iteration.

selfTest.q: What does a smaller token budget cost?
selfTest.a: The new request's prefill spreads over more iterations, so its TTFT grows. Decode protection is paid in prefill latency.

selfTest.q: Decode batch grows from 1 to 32 at fixed lengths. What happens to per-step time and to tokens per second?
selfTest.a: Per-step time rises sublinearly while weight reuse climbs, so tokens per second rise until the work turns compute-bound or hits capacity.

study.title: TTFT, ITL and end-to-end definitions
study.locator: Latency Metrics (pp. 150 to 151): Figure 4-9 with TTFT as prefill work, ITL as decode work, and the end-to-end formula over N generated tokens
study.depth: Use the definitions and the final simplified forms. The printed ITL middle expression with a subtracted detokenization term is garbled; read it as one decode step plus its detokenization.

study.title: Bench-side TTFT, ITL and TPOT
study.locator: Understanding the Latency Metrics: bench-side TTFT, per-gap ITL and per-request TPOT with the speculative-decoding bundled-tokens example

focus: Engine-side intervals and bench-side metrics differ by construction. The engine measures queue, prefill and decode between core events; the bench measures TTFT, gaps and TPOT at the client, including network and streaming.
ITL records each gap between streamed outputs, while TPOT amortizes one request's decode time over its tokens. They agree for one-token outputs and diverge when one output bundles several tokens.
Sampling, detokenization and streaming sit after the last model kernel of each step. A ragged gap series with fast kernels points at these parts, not at attention.
Preemption re-enters the intervals: a preempted request restarts prefill, so its TTFT and decode spans include the repeated work.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the engine events and the five intervals for a request that queue-waits, prefills, decodes three tokens and finishes, then state the bench-side TTFT, the two ITL samples and the TPOT for N = 4 output tokens.
traps: Averaging ITL samples across requests with different output lengths and calling it TPOT. Mean of gaps weights long requests more; per-request TPOT weights requests equally.
Comparing engine prefill time with bench TTFT directly. TTFT adds queueing, tokenization, network and streaming around the engine spans.
Trusting TPOT for single-token requests. vLLM records zero TPOT when there is at most one output token, and bench statistics exclude those requests.

selfTest.q: A request generates 5 tokens with TTFT 100 ms and end-to-end 180 ms. What is its TPOT, and how many ITL samples does the bench record?
selfTest.a: TPOT is (180 - 100) / (5 - 1) = 20 ms per token. The bench records 4 ITL gap samples.

selfTest.q: With speculative decoding, one streamed output carries three tokens after a 40 ms gap. How do ITL and TPOT treat those tokens?
selfTest.a: ITL records one 40 ms gap and adds no zero gaps for the bundled tokens. TPOT divides the request's decode time over all three tokens.

selfTest.q: Queue time dominates a slow TTFT while prefill time is flat. What do you fix first?
selfTest.a: Admission, scheduling or load, not kernels. The model execution is fine; the request waited.

selfTest.q: Why can two runs of the same prompt show different TTFT with identical prefill time?
selfTest.a: TTFT includes queueing, tokenization, scheduling and host overhead, which vary with server state even when the kernels do not.

units.title: Device synchronization, warmup, compilation and cold versus warm state
outcomes: Explain why host timers need device synchronization and what stream-ordered event semantics guarantee.
Separate warmup, compilation and graph-capture state from steady-state timing.
Design a cold-versus-warm comparison that fixes model, cache and workload state.
units.why: Asynchronous launch makes naive timers measure submission, not execution. Every timing in this section stands or falls on synchronization and warm state.

next.note: Run warmed, synchronized baselines across sweeps and shapes.
Separate warm-state effects from trial variance.

study.locator: Profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute (pp. 969 to 973): per-stream naming, NVTX Prefill and Decode step ranges, and the tightest scope around encode

study.locator: Before Benchmarking: persistence mode with sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1, clock reset with sudo nvidia-smi -rgc, power limits and boost settings

study.title: Cache-state control for latency runs
study.locator: Online Benchmark warning on prefix-cache reuse across repeated runs, with varying the seed, restarting the server or resetting caches between runs

focus: Treat the Timed boundaries, asynchronous launch and event timing unit and the Warmup, compilation, allocator and cache state unit as read. This unit applies them to serving runs.
Kernel launches return before the work finishes. A host timer without synchronization measures queueing into the driver, and only stream-ordered events or a synchronize call bracket the device work.
First runs include compilation, graph capture, allocator setup and cold caches. Warm every shape you will time, then discard the warmup before recording.

Cold versus warm is a comparison of stated states: model weights resident or not, graphs captured or not, prefix cache empty or populated, clocks settled or not. Name all four before quoting either number.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, list the five warm states that a first vLLM request passes through before steady state, and write the synchronized timing pattern that brackets one decode step without including queue submission.
traps: Timing a range that includes the first-ever request and calling it the baseline. Compilation and capture dominate it; it is a startup measurement, not a serving one.
Reusing prompts across repeated latency runs with prefix caching on. Later runs hit the cache and look faster without any real change.
Comparing a cold run at settled clocks with a warm run after thermal throttling started. Clocks and temperature are part of the state; record both.

selfTest.q: Why does an unsynchronized host timer under-report GPU work?
selfTest.a: Launches are asynchronous, so the timer stops at submission. The device work continues after the host proceeds.

selfTest.q: What does a stream-ordered event pair guarantee that a host timer does not?
selfTest.a: It brackets work in the device's own order on that stream, so queueing and overlap on other streams cannot leak into the interval.

selfTest.q: Which states must a warmup cover before a latency baseline?
selfTest.a: Model weights resident, compilation and graph capture done, allocator settled, caches at their declared state, and clocks settled. Time only after all of them.

selfTest.q: Two latency runs differ only in that the second reuses the first run's prompts. What explains a faster second run?
selfTest.a: Prefix-cache hits from the first run's KV blocks, not faster execution. Vary the seed or reset the server for a clean comparison.

study.locator: Running With Sampling Parameters with the temperature, top-p and top-k example; Understanding the Latency Metrics for requests that generate at most one token

study.title: The fairness checklist
study.locator: Before-you-publish checklist: fixed input and output lengths, p50 with p95 and p99, TTFT and ITL kept separate, pinned versions with exact commands

focus: Build on the Proving the cache correct unit: token identity plus a logits tolerance is the correctness gate, and this unit adds the serving comparison contract around it.
Greedy means temperature at 0, which vLLM treats as greedy below 1e-5. Seeded sampling means a fixed seed at temperature above 0, compared by distribution over repeats, not by single outputs.
Output limits and stop strings change the amount of work. Fix max_tokens, ignore_eos, stop and stop_token_ids identically, or the faster run may simply have generated less.
Batch sizes, kernel paths and cache states can move outputs and timings. State them in the contract and re-verify identity whenever any of them changes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the full comparison contract for two engine settings: identical prompts, SamplingParams(temperature=0, seed=1) with fixed max_tokens and stop behavior, and declared cache state. Then show greedy token identity across reruns and seeded-sampling distributional agreement across repeats.
traps: Assuming the bench seed fixes engine sampling. The bench seed samples the dataset; engine sampling needs its own seed in SamplingParams or a server seed.
Comparing a run that stopped early on EOS with one that ran to the token limit. Different output counts mean different decode work, not different speed.
Claiming determinism from one identical rerun. Greedy identity needs repeats across the batch sizes and cache states you will actually compare.

selfTest.q: Why must max_tokens and stop behavior match before comparing TPOT?
selfTest.a: They set how many decode steps run. A shorter output does fewer steps, so its TPOT can differ without any execution change.

selfTest.q: How do you compare two sampled configurations without requiring identical tokens?
selfTest.a: Fix the seed and compare output distributions over repeats, such as acceptance rates or score histograms, with identical prompts, limits and cache state.

selfTest.q: Greedy outputs match at batch size 1 but differ at batch size 8. What broke?
selfTest.a: The comparison contract. A kernel path, scheduling or cache behavior changed with batch size, so identity must be re-established there, not assumed.

selfTest.q: What does vLLM do with a small positive temperature below 1e-2?
selfTest.a: It warns and clamps it up to 1e-2. Use exactly 0 for greedy and a fixed seed for reproducible sampling.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the identical-output gate every timing comparison must pass, with fixed prompts, limits, stop behavior, seed and cache state.

study.title: Synthetic datasets with fixed shapes
study.locator: Preparing a Dataset with the task_id, prompt or input_ids and output_tokens schema, and the token-norm-dist synthetic example at input-mean 128 with output-mean 128

focus: The single-request cell comes first and stays fixed: one prompt shape, warmed state, identical-output contract, raw per-request results kept.

Sweep one variable at a time: concurrency with fixed rate, then rate with fixed concurrency. The knee where throughput stops rising while latency degrades is the result; points past preemption are not publishable.
Every matrix cell fixes input length, output length, batch size, sampling and cache state. A cell that changes two of them explains nothing.
Keep TTFT and ITL separate in every cell and every sweep. Blended latency hides whether the limit is prefill, decode or queueing.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the sweep plan for your model: the single-request cell, the concurrency ladder, the request-rate ladder, and three shape-matrix cells with every fixed field named. Then run the single-request cell with vllm bench latency --input-len 32 --output-len 128 --batch-size 8.
traps: Measuring at the preemption point and reporting it as capacity. When waiting requests climb and TTFT spikes, stop and tune admission and chunking first.
Sweeping with uniform synthetic lengths and claiming production coverage. Fixed shapes give comparability, but real distributions still need their own run.
Changing output length across cells to save time. Shorter outputs do less decode work, so the cells are no longer comparable.

selfTest.q: What makes the single-request baseline a baseline rather than an anecdote?
selfTest.a: Fixed lengths, warmup, the identical-output contract and retained raw results, so any later change can rerun the same cell.

selfTest.q: Throughput flattens while p99 climbs steeply with concurrency. Where are you?
selfTest.a: At the saturation knee. Report the knee; further points measure overload behavior, not serving capacity.

selfTest.q: Why sweep rate and concurrency separately instead of together?
selfTest.a: They stress different limits: rate stresses arrivals and queueing, concurrency stresses resident batch and memory. Joint sweeps confound them.

selfTest.q: What does vllm bench latency fix that vllm bench serve leaves open?
selfTest.a: Latency runs one fixed batch of fixed input and output lengths for phase timing. Serve replays arrivals over time for endpoint behavior under load.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the sweep harness with the single-request cell, the concurrency and rate ladders, and the shape matrix with raw results per cell.
units.stopWhen: Your matrix reruns cell-for-cell with identical contracts, and you can point to the knee in your own sweep data.

fit.note: The bench CLI, the TTFT sweep sessions and the synthetic-dataset checklist cover all three topics at measure depth, with practice in the mini-project harness.
